en: To attack violently, physically or with criticism
hook: ASSAIL: ASSAULT someone.
story: Assail. When the young cricket captain dropped an easy catch in the final, social media exploded. Thousands of fans assailed him with insults, cartoons, and angry videos. Even former players criticized him on television. He was assailed: attacked violently with criticism. The word can also be physical, as when soldiers assail a fort, or mental, as when doubts assail you at night. Assail and assault come from the same Latin root, meaning to leap upon. Synonyms: attack, besiege, lambaste.

gre.s: Critics were quick to ____ the report, questioning its methods, dismissing its data, and even impugning the integrity of its authors.
gre.clue: even impugning the integrity of its authors

en: Well-meaning and kind; charitable
hook: BENE-VOLENT: wishing (vol) good (bene).
story: Benevolent. Every winter, Ishita's grandfather, a retired schoolteacher in Rangpur, spends part of his pension on blankets. He walks from house to house in the poorest part of town, handing them out quietly, without taking photographs or telling anyone. He is benevolent: well-meaning, kind, and charitable. Bene means good and vol means wish, as in volunteer: a benevolent person wishes others well. Its opposite is malevolent, wishing harm. Synonyms: kind, generous, philanthropic.

gre.s: Far from being the ____ patron he appeared to be in public, the landlord privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent.
gre.clue: privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent

en: To scold or criticize angrily
hook: BE-RATE: give someone a terrible RATING, loudly.
story: Berate. Rumana's bus was stuck in traffic, and she arrived at the office forty minutes late. Her boss was waiting at the door. In front of the entire team, he berated her, shouting about responsibility, discipline, and wasted money for a full ten minutes. Rumana's face burned. To berate is to scold or criticize angrily, usually at length. In old English, to rate someone meant to scold them, and berate makes it harsher. Synonyms: scold, upbraid, rebuke.

gre.s: The coach was known to ____ his players loudly in front of the crowd, so the team was astonished when he met their worst defeat with quiet encouragement.
gre.clue: astonished when he met their worst defeat with quiet encouragement

en: Able to float; cheerful and optimistic
hook: BUOYANT: like a BUOY, always floating up.
story: Buoyant. On a trip to the Sundarbans, Anika was nervous about the boat ride. The guide handed her a bright orange life jacket and explained that it was buoyant: able to float, and able to keep her floating too. Then she noticed the guide himself. After twenty years on the river, he was still singing and joking, buoyant in spirit: cheerful and optimistic. Both senses mean staying up. A buoy is a floating marker in a harbour. Synonyms: floating, cheerful, upbeat.

gre.s: Investors remained ____ despite the gloomy forecasts, convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months and reward those who held their nerve.
gre.clue: convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months

en: To support or strengthen
hook: BUTTRESS: the stone supports holding up a cathedral wall.
story: Buttress. The old mosque in Farhan's town had a cracked wall that leaned a little more each monsoon. Engineers built thick brick supports against it from the outside, and the wall stopped moving. Those supports are called buttresses. As a verb, to buttress is to support or strengthen, and it is often used for arguments: Sara buttressed her thesis with data from forty villages. Gothic cathedrals in Europe are famous for their flying buttresses. Synonyms: bolster, reinforce, shore up.

gre.s: Knowing that the jury would distrust a single witness, the lawyer sought to ____ her argument with testimony from three independent experts.
gre.clue: Knowing that the jury would distrust a single witness

en: To accept or overlook wrong behavior
hook: CONDONE: CON + DONE, letting a con be done without objection.
story: Condone. During an exam, Sara saw her classmates passing answers to each other. The invigilator saw it too, yet he simply looked out of the window and said nothing. By ignoring it, he condoned the cheating: he accepted or overlooked wrong behaviour as if it were acceptable. Condone does not mean approving enthusiastically; it means letting something wrong pass. A school that never punishes bullying condones it. Synonyms: overlook, excuse, tolerate. Its opposite is condemn.

gre.s: By remaining silent while his colleagues falsified the data, the director effectively chose to ____ the fraud, even though he never took part in it himself.
gre.clue: By remaining silent

en: To violate a law or rule
hook: CONTRA-VENE: come (vene) AGAINST (contra) the rule.
story: Contravene. A factory owner near the Buriganga river was quietly pumping untreated waste into the water at night. Environmental inspectors took samples, traced the hidden pipe, and fined him heavily. His actions contravened the environmental protection law: they violated it. Contra means against and ven means come, as in convene: to contravene is to come against a rule. It can also mean to contradict a statement. Synonyms: violate, breach, infringe. Its opposite is to obey or comply.

gre.s: Although the company insisted that its new policy was perfectly legal, inspectors found that it would ____ at least three provisions of the labour code.
gre.clue: Although the company insisted that its new policy was perfectly legal

en: To publicly declare something wrong or evil
hook: DE-NOUNCE: ANNOUNCE it's bad.
story: Denounce. At a public meeting, the headmistress of a village school stood up in front of the elders and the local chairman. She announced that a powerful family had been marrying off fourteen-year-old girls, and declared that it was illegal and wrong. She had denounced the practice: publicly declared it wrong or evil. Denounce can also mean to inform against someone, as in denouncing a traitor. The noun is denunciation. Synonyms: condemn, decry, censure.

gre.s: Human rights groups were quick to ____ the arrests, calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics.
gre.clue: calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics

en: Ruling with absolute and often cruel power
hook: DESPOTIC: a DESPOT, an all-powerful tyrant.
story: Despotic. In a history class, Nabil read about an ancient king who executed anyone who criticized him, seized farmers' harvests whenever he wished, and made every law himself, with no council and no court to stop him. His teacher called the king's rule despotic: absolute and often cruel. A despot is a ruler with total power. The word can describe a boss or a parent too: a despotic manager tolerates no disagreement. Synonyms: tyrannical, autocratic, dictatorial.

gre.s: The new leader, who had promised a return to democracy, soon proved just as ____ as his predecessor, jailing critics and ruling by decree.
gre.clue: jailing critics and ruling by decree

en: To depart from an established course or norm
hook: DE-VIA-TE: off the road (via).
story: Deviate. Every morning, Zayan's father drives the same route to his office in Motijheel: same roads, same turns, same tea stall. One day a procession blocked the main road, and he was forced to deviate from his route, taking narrow lanes he had never seen. To deviate is to depart from an established course or norm. Statisticians measure standard deviation: how far values stray from the average. A deviant is someone who departs from social norms. Synonyms: diverge, stray, digress.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the accident occurred because the crew chose to ____ from standard procedures, skipping two of the required safety checks before takeoff.
gre.clue: skipping two of the required safety checks

en: Impartial; not influenced by personal advantage
hook: GRE trick: DISINTERESTED = no personal INTEREST (stake). Not the same as uninterested!
story: Disinterested. Two brothers in Tanvir's village were fighting over their late father's land. Neither trusted the other's friends to settle it. Finally they asked the old schoolteacher, who owned no land and was related to neither of them. He was disinterested: impartial, with nothing personal to gain. Careful: disinterested does not mean bored. That is uninterested. A disinterested judge is the best kind; an uninterested judge is asleep. Synonyms: impartial, unbiased, neutral.

gre.s: Because neither mediator had any financial stake in the outcome, both companies accepted them as ____ arbiters of the dispute.
gre.clue: had any financial stake in the outcome

en: To increase rapidly in intensity or seriousness
hook: ESCALATE: like an ESCALATOR, going up and up.
story: Escalate. It started with a small argument between two rickshaw pullers about who had the right of way. One shouted, and the other shouted louder. Passengers joined in, shopkeepers took sides, and within ten minutes a crowd of fifty was pushing and yelling. The argument had escalated: increased rapidly in intensity and seriousness. Think of an escalator, carrying you up step by step without stopping. Its opposite is de-escalate, to calm things down. Synonyms: intensify, mount, spiral.

gre.s: What began as a minor quarrel over a parking space threatened to ____ into a brawl as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides.
gre.clue: as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides

en: To drive out an evil spirit; to get rid of something troubling
hook: EXORCISE: EXIT the demons.
story: Exorcise. In old village tales, when someone behaved strangely, the family might call a healer to exorcise the evil spirit: to drive it out with prayers and rituals. Today the word is often used for troubling memories. After failing his first GRE attempt, Rafi felt haunted by it for months. Half a year later he scored three hundred and thirty, and finally exorcised that failure. Do not confuse exorcise with exercise. Synonyms: banish, expel, purge.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the memory of her humiliating defeat, the champion trained harder than ever and returned to win the title the following year.
gre.clue: humiliating defeat

en: Fussy and hard to please; requiring great attention to detail
hook: FINICKY: FINE details only — picky.
story: Finicky. Mitu's little brother is the most finicky eater in the family. He will not eat rice if it touches the dal. He removes every piece of onion from his curry and refuses fish if he spots a single bone. Feeding him takes an hour. Finicky means fussy and hard to please. It can also describe a task that needs great attention to detail, like repairing a finicky old watch. Synonyms: fussy, picky, fastidious. Its opposite is easygoing.

gre.s: The critic was notoriously ____ about food, sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool or whose garnish sat slightly off centre.
gre.clue: sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool

en: To prevent something from succeeding; a person who contrasts with another
hook: FOIL: wrap the plan in FOIL so it can't work.
story: Foil. Three thieves planned to rob a mobile phone shop in Farmgate at midnight. But the night guard noticed their van circling the block, called the police, and switched on every light. The thieves fled empty-handed. The guard had foiled their plan: prevented it from succeeding. As a noun, a foil is a character who contrasts with another, making their qualities stand out. Steady, ordinary Watson is the perfect foil for brilliant Sherlock Holmes. Synonyms: thwart, frustrate, stymie.

gre.s: An alert bank clerk managed to ____ the robbery by quietly pressing a silent alarm, and the police arrived before the gang could reach the vault.
gre.clue: by quietly pressing a silent alarm

en: Twisted together; closely connected
hook: INTER-TWINED: TWINE twisted together.
story: Intertwined. Behind Priya's grandmother's house stand two old trees, a mango and a jackfruit, planted on the same day sixty years ago. Their branches have grown around each other so closely that nobody can say where one ends and the other begins. They are intertwined: twisted together. The word is often used for lives and ideas too: in Bangladesh, the histories of the language movement and independence are deeply intertwined, closely connected. Synonyms: entwined, interwoven, interlinked.

gre.s: In the novelist's vision, the fates of the two families are so ____ that no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other.
gre.clue: no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other

en: To flood; to overwhelm with too much of something
hook: INUNDATE: IN + UNDA (wave). Waves pour in.
story: Inundate. Every monsoon, the river near Joya's village rises above its banks and inundates the rice fields: it floods them completely. Only the tops of the banana trees remain visible. The word also has a figurative sense. When Joya posted her free GRE notes online, she was inundated with messages: hundreds of requests arrived, far more than she could ever answer. Unda is Latin for wave: to inundate is to cover with waves. Synonyms: flood, swamp, overwhelm.

gre.s: The monsoon rains that year were heavy enough to ____ the low-lying villages, forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground with whatever they could carry.
gre.clue: forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground

en: Impossible to break or contradict
hook: IRON-CLAD: covered in IRON armor.
story: Ironclad. Before investing his savings in his cousin's business, Kamal insisted on a contract. A lawyer drafted it carefully: every payment, every date, and every penalty was spelled out, with signatures and witnesses. When a dispute arose years later, there was no loophole to exploit. The contract was ironclad: impossible to break or contradict. The word first described warships covered in iron plates. An ironclad alibi or an ironclad guarantee cannot be broken. Synonyms: airtight, watertight, unassailable.

gre.s: The prosecution believed its case was ____, yet a single overlooked receipt was enough to establish the defendant's alibi and collapse the entire argument.
gre.clue: yet a single overlooked receipt was enough

en: To put someone or something in danger
hook: JEOPARDIZE: put it in JEOPARDY.
story: Jeopardize. Two months before his final exams, Arif started playing online games until four every morning. His grades fell, he missed classes, and the scholarship committee sent him a warning letter. His habit was jeopardizing his scholarship: putting it in danger. Jeopardy means danger. It comes from an old French phrase for an evenly divided game, which you could just as easily lose as win. Something in jeopardy is at risk. Synonyms: endanger, imperil, threaten.

gre.s: Officials warned that any further delay would ____ the entire bridge project, since the foreign loan would be withdrawn if construction had not begun by March.
gre.clue: since the foreign loan would be withdrawn

en: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
hook: MERCURIAL: like MERCURY (liquid metal), never stays still.
story: Mercurial. Nobody in the office knew what mood the director would be in. On Monday he joked and bought everyone sweets. On Tuesday morning he shouted at the cleaner. By Tuesday afternoon he was laughing again. He was mercurial: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood. Mercury, the liquid metal in old thermometers, slides and shifts quickly, and the Roman god Mercury was a swift, tricky messenger. Synonyms: volatile, fickle, capricious. Its opposite is steady.

gre.s: Her ____ temperament made her a difficult colleague: she could be warmly encouraging at breakfast and coldly dismissive by lunch.
gre.clue: warmly encouraging at breakfast and coldly dismissive by lunch

en: Not aware of what is happening around one
hook: OBLIVIOUS: in OBLIVION, totally unaware.
story: Oblivious. Mahin was so absorbed in his vocabulary app at Kamalapur station that he did not hear the announcements, did not notice the crowd boarding, and did not see his train pull away. When he finally looked up, the platform was empty. He had been oblivious: not aware of what was happening around him. Oblivious is usually followed by to or of. A related word is oblivion, the state of being forgotten. Synonyms: unaware, heedless, unmindful.

gre.s: Engrossed in her phone, the pedestrian remained completely ____ to the truck bearing down on her until a stranger grabbed her arm and pulled her back.
gre.clue: until a stranger grabbed her arm and pulled her back

en: To carry out a harmful, illegal, or immoral act
hook: PERPETRATE: a PERP (criminal) does it.
story: Perpetrate. For months, a gang in Sabbir's town sent fake lottery messages, telling people they had won a car and asking for a small processing fee. Hundreds of families lost money. When police finally arrested the men who had perpetrated the fraud, the town celebrated. To perpetrate is to carry out a harmful, illegal, or immoral act. The person who does it is the perpetrator. Do not confuse it with perpetuate, which means to keep something going. Synonyms: commit, carry out.

gre.s: Although the soldiers claimed they were only following orders, the tribunal held that those who ____ such atrocities bear personal responsibility for them.
gre.clue: the soldiers claimed they were only following orders

en: Sounding sad and mournful
hook: PLAINTIVE: like a PLAINT, a sad complaint.
story: Plaintive. Late one night near the Padma, Tania heard a boatman singing a bhatiali song as he rowed home. His voice was slow and low, full of longing for a home and a love far away. Even without catching every word, she felt like crying. The song was plaintive: sounding sad and mournful. Plaintive shares a root with complaint and plaintiff: a plaintive sound is like a gentle lament. Synonyms: mournful, wistful, doleful. Its opposite is cheerful.

gre.s: From the abandoned house drifted the ____ notes of a flute, so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent.
gre.clue: so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent

en: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or deep emotion
hook: POIGNANT: POINTED, it pierces your heart.
story: Poignant. At the airport, Imran watched an old man hugging his son, who was leaving to work abroad for five years. The father pressed a small packet of homemade pitha into his son's hand and said nothing. Neither of them could speak. It was a poignant moment: evoking a keen sense of sadness and deep emotion. The g is silent: POY-nyant. It comes from a French word meaning to prick: a poignant scene pierces the heart. Synonyms: moving, touching, heart-rending.

gre.s: The film's final scene is quietly ____: the elderly widower, alone in the empty house, still sets out two cups of tea each morning out of habit.
gre.clue: alone in the empty house, still sets out two cups of tea each morning out of habit

en: In a state of inactivity or dormancy
hook: QUIESCENT: QUIET and resting.
story: Quiescent. For eight months, the workers' union in Nadia's district held no meetings, filed no complaints, and organized no protests. Observers thought it had disappeared. Then wages were cut, and overnight it came roaring back to life. During those months it had been quiescent: inactive or dormant, but not dead. Quiescent shares a root with quiet. Doctors call a disease quiescent when it is present but causing no symptoms. Synonyms: dormant, inactive, latent.

gre.s: The volcano had been ____ for nearly three centuries, so few residents took the scientists' warnings seriously when the ground began to rumble.
gre.clue: for nearly three centuries

en: To say something again, often for emphasis
hook: RE-ITERATE: say it again and again (iterate).
story: Reiterate. At the start of every class, Shuvo's maths teacher wrote the same sentence on the board: 'Read the question twice.' Students rolled their eyes, but every week she reiterated it, because every week someone lost marks by misreading. To reiterate is to say something again, often for emphasis. Iterate already means to repeat, so reiterate means repeating once more. Politicians reiterate their positions, and teachers reiterate rules. Synonyms: repeat, restate, emphasize.

gre.s: Because so many students had ignored the first notice, the principal felt obliged to ____ the warning in a second, more strongly worded letter.
gre.clue: Because so many students had ignored the first notice

en: To become less intense, violent, or severe
hook: SUB-SIDE: sinking down (sub) to the side.
story: Subside. The fever started on Monday night. Lamia's temperature climbed to a hundred and three, and her mother sat beside her with wet cloths until dawn. By Wednesday the fever began to subside, and by Friday Lamia was hungry again. To subside is to become less intense, violent, or severe. Floods subside, anger subsides, and noise subsides. Sub means under and sid means settle: things sink back down. Synonyms: abate, recede, diminish.

gre.s: The villagers camped on the embankment for three days, waiting for the floodwaters to ____ so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes.
gre.clue: so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes

en: To include or absorb something into a larger category
hook: SUB-SUME: SUM it UNDER a larger heading.
story: Subsume. When the government merged three small banks into one large national bank, the old names disappeared from the signboards, and customers of all three became customers of the new bank. The small banks had been subsumed: included or absorbed into something larger. In the same way, mango is subsumed under the category of fruit. Sub means under, and sume means take, as in assume and consume: to subsume is to take something under a larger umbrella. Synonyms: absorb, incorporate, encompass.

gre.s: Some linguists think it misleading to ____ Chittagonian into the broader category of Bengali dialects, since speakers of the two can barely understand each other.
gre.clue: since speakers of the two can barely understand each other

en: To overcome a difficulty or obstacle
hook: SUR-MOUNT: climb OVER the MOUNTain.
story: Surmount. Babu was born on a char, a sandy island in the Jamuna that floods every year. His school had no electricity, so he studied by a kerosene lamp, and more than once the river washed away his books. Yet he surmounted every obstacle and won a place at a top engineering university. To surmount is to overcome a difficulty or obstacle. Sur means over and mount means climb, as in mountain: to surmount is to climb over. Synonyms: overcome, conquer, transcend.

gre.s: Experts doubted that the climbers could ____ the final ice wall, which had turned back every previous expedition; yet the team reached the summit before noon.
gre.clue: which had turned back every previous expedition

en: Only slightly related; diverging from the main topic
hook: TANGENTIAL: like a TANGENT line, it only touches the circle at one point.
story: Tangential. Professor Haque began a lecture on climate policy. Ten minutes later he was talking about his childhood in Barisal, then about the best way to cook hilsa, then about a cricket match from 1999. The students exchanged glances. His remarks were tangential: only slightly related to the main topic. In geometry, a tangent touches a circle at a single point and then heads off in another direction. Going off on a tangent means wandering from the subject. Synonyms: peripheral, incidental, digressive.

gre.s: The committee found most of the testimony ____ to the central question, since witnesses spent hours on matters only loosely connected to the contract.
gre.clue: matters only loosely connected to the contract
